passages.text: Chemical properties and colors of fermenting materials in salmon fish sauce production

This data article reports the chemical properties (moisture, pH, salinity, and soluble solid content) and colors of fermenting materials in salmon fish sauce products. <sentence_start/>The fish sauce was produced by mixing salt with differing proportions of raw salmon materials and fermenting for three months; the salmon materials comprised flesh, viscera, an inedible portion, and soft roe. <sentence_start/>Chemical properties and colors of the unrefined fish sauce (<italic toggle="yes">moromi</italic>), and the refined fish sauce, were analyzed at one, two, and three months following the start of fermentation. <sentence_start/>Data determined for all products are provided in table format.
The data would be available as reference for culinary studies on fish sauces and related products.
The data will be useful for nutritional assessments of fish sauce products based on their chemical properties.
The data will be useful for discussions on the metabolism of fish sauce chemical components during fermentation.

This article presents data on moisture, pH, salinity, and soluble solid content of unrefined fish sauce, (<italic toggle="yes">moromi</italic>; Table 1) and filtered fish sauce (Table 2) throughout the fermentation process; we also report colorimetric data (Table 3 for <italic toggle="yes">moromi</italic>; Table 4 for fish sauce). <sentence_start/>Japanese terms in this article are explained in Table S1.

We used female ‘<italic toggle="yes">Bunasake’</italic> and ‘<italic toggle="yes">Ginke’</italic> chum salmon (<italic toggle="yes">Oncorhynchus keta</italic>) from Hokkaido, Japan. <italic toggle="yes">‘Bunasake</italic>’, which is chum salmon after the egg-laying period, has a low market value, because these fish abstain from eating during their pre-spawning run upstream, and the fat in their flesh is depleted. <sentence_start/>On the other hand, ‘<italic toggle="yes">Ginke’</italic>, which is chum salmon before the period of migration and spawning, has high market value, because the flesh of these fish is relatively high in fat content. <sentence_start/>We also used <italic toggle="yes">shio-koji</italic>, a salt-marinated rice malt, as the fermentation starter. <sentence_start/>For the color measurement, the <italic toggle="yes">L</italic>* value that represents brightness, <italic toggle="yes">a</italic>* value that represents red/green and <italic toggle="yes">b</italic>* that represents yellow/blue were employed to assess lightness and degree of color shift of the products, respectively.

The ‘<italic toggle="yes">Bunasake’</italic> salmon and ‘<italic toggle="yes">Ginke’</italic> salmon were purchased at a local market in Abashiri, Hokkaido. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Shio-koji</italic> containing 12.3% salt (Kurashige jozo Co. Ltd., Abashiri Japan) and salt (Shokuen, The Salt Industry Center of Japan, Tokyo, Japan) were used for fish sauce production.

Raw salmon was dissected into flesh, viscera, an inedible portion, and soft roe. <sentence_start/>Each portion was minced using a food processor. <sentence_start/>Each minced portion and salt were mixed at various proportions (Table S2), and left for three months in a 37 °C constant temperature incubator (DG-82, Yamato, Japan). <sentence_start/>The chemical properties and colors of the <italic toggle="yes">moromi</italic> (unrefined fish sauce) and filtered fish sauce were measured at one, two, and three months following the start of fermentation.

Salinity and pH were measured using a salt meter (B-721; HORIBA, Japan) and a pH meter (D-52; HORIBA). <sentence_start/>Water content was measured according to the methods published by the Association of Official Analytical Chemists <citation rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr" count="1">[1]</citation>, <citation rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr" count="1">[2]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Soluble solid content (%) was defined as content excluding the water content. <sentence_start/>Unsalted soluble solid content (%) was defined as the soluble solid content excluding the salt content.

The colors of dried salmon products were measured using a colorimeter (CR-400; Konica Minolta, Tokyo, Japan). <sentence_start/>The measured data were expressed in Lab color space in which the tree dimensions L* for lightness, and a* and b* for the color opponents green/red and blue/yellow.
